The company is essentially the technology arm of **Quality Surgical Management (QSM)**, a wound care services company founded in 1999 (some sources say 1996) by Dr. Steven Magilen, a general surgeon with 35+ years of wound care experience. QSM provides bedside wound care management in skilled nursing facilities (SNFs) and assisted living facilities across six states. QSM is the sole user of QSmartCare — the real-world testing report explicitly states \"Our EHR is only used by one healthcare provider (ourselves).\"\n     9→\n    10→QSM is a small private company with approximately 75 employees. It has treated over 171,000 patients across 605 facilities. The company raised less than $5M in a single funding round (2020). QSM is JCAHO-certified and is headquartered in Hollywood, Florida. Dr. Magilen serves as both the CEO/Medical Director of QSM and the developer contact for the certified EHR product.\n    11→\n    12→This is a classic case of a clinical practice that built its own specialty EHR for internal use and then pursued ONC certification. QSmartCare was developed \"by and for wound care physicians\" over 30 years, long before it was formally certified (January 2022).\n    13→\n    14→## Product: QSmartCare\n    15→\n    16→CHPL ID: 10803\n    17→\n    18→### What It Is\n    19→\n    20→QSmartCare is a cloud-based (SaaS) wound care EHR purpose-built for documenting and managing wound care encounters in skilled nursing facilities. It is not a general-purpose EHR — it is a specialty system designed around the workflow of wound care physicians, PAs, and NPs who travel to SNFs to provide bedside wound care services.\n    21→\n    22→The certified module appears to be the whole product. There is a web application (app.qsmartcare.com) and a companion iOS mobile app (QSmartCare on the App Store, published by Quality Surgical Management Inc.) that allows providers to view schedules, access patient details, and capture wound photographs with auto edge detection. The mobile app connects to the web portal.\n    23→\n    24→### Users & Market\n    25→\n    26→**Primary users**: QSM's own wound care providers (physicians, PAs, NPs) and administrative staff (billers, coders, administrators). The SED intended user description is \"Nurses, Physicians, & Staff.\"\n    27→\n    28→**Clinical setting**: Wound care provided at the bedside in skilled nursing facilities and assisted living facilities. QSM clinicians travel to partner facilities to provide wound treatment — the EHR is used during these visits and for follow-up documentation.\n    29→\n    30→**Scale**: QSM reports serving 605 facilities and treating 171,129 patients. However, the real-world testing report reveals that many certified features (Direct messaging, eCQM submission, immunization entry) had zero actual usage in CY 2023. This suggests the EHR's day-to-day use is narrowly focused on wound care documentation rather than the full spectrum of certified capabilities.\n    31→\n    32→**Customer base**: QSmartCare is an internal tool — QSM is the only customer. It is not marketed or sold to external healthcare organizations.\n    33→\n    34→### Modules & Functionality\n    35→\n    36→Based on vendor materials, the product website, CHPL certification criteria, and integration documentation:\n    37→\n    38→**Core wound care charting**: The primary function. The website emphasizes \"accelerated charting\" with an \"intelligent workflow and interface\" to reduce repetitive documentation. The charting module is described as packed with \"time-saving functions\" for fast documentation. This is the central purpose of the system — wound assessment, documentation, and treatment tracking.\n    39→\n    40→**Wound photography**: The mobile app supports capturing wound photographs with auto edge detection and image cropping for document uploads. This is a key feature for wound care — visual documentation of wound healing progress.\n    41→\n    42→**Clinical Decision Support**: The system has CDS engines with configurable rules that \"provide suggestions based on standard rule defined and option for the new rule configuration on the application settings.\" Certified for (a)(1)–(a)(5) clinical criteria.\n    43→\n    44→**Care Plans**: A care plan module that \"aligns and archives the treatment plan with the patient's objectives, and formulates documentation into the pattern of a Care Plan.\" This is central to wound care management — treatment plans, goals, and progress tracking.\n    45→\n    46→**Medication management**: The website states QSmartCare \"makes the data entry and management of patient medications easy.\" The ONC costs page references NewCrop as a third-party integration, indicating e-prescribing capability. Certified for (b)(11) — clinical information reconciliation.\n    47→\n    48→**Patient portal**: Certified for (e)(1) — view, download, transmit. There is a patient login page at qsmartcare.com/patient/. The real-world testing results suggest this has low actual usage.\n    49→\n    50→**Care transitions / Interoperability**: Certified for (b)(1)–(b)(3) — transitions of care via C-CDA and Direct messaging (using Data Motion as a third-party service). The MatrixCare integration is particularly notable: QSM has a bidirectional integration with MatrixCare (a major SNF EHR) where patient face sheet data flows automatically into QSmartCare, and wound documentation flows back into MatrixCare. This is the primary interoperability workflow — exchanging data with the host facility's EHR.\n    51→\n    52→**FHIR API**: Certified for (g)(7)–(g)(10). The API documentation shows a FHIR R4 API conforming to US Core 3.1, plus a legacy Patient API that returns C-CDA XML. The FHIR API exposes 21 resources including AllergyIntolerance, CarePlan, CareTeam, Condition, Device, DiagnosticReport, DocumentReference, Encounter, Goal, Immunization, MedicationRequest, Observation, Organization, Patient, Practitioner, PractitionerRole, Location, and Procedure.\n    53→\n    54→**Public health reporting**: Certified for (f)(1) immunization registry and (f)(2) syndromic surveillance, though real-world testing found zero actual usage of these features. This makes sense — wound care providers in SNFs are unlikely to be doing immunizations or reporting syndromic surveillance.\n    55→\n    56→**Clinical quality measures**: Certified for (c)(1)–(c)(3) — CQM recording, exporting, and reporting. Again, real-world testing showed no actual eCQM submissions.\n    57→\n    58→**EHI export**: Certified for (b)(10). The export page describes PDF (human-readable) and JSON (machine-readable) formats, with both single-patient and bulk multi-patient export capabilities. Accessible via Patient > CCDA > Export menu. Requires Author-level permissions.\n    59→\n    60→### Data & Content\n    61→\n    62→Based on the FHIR API resources, certified criteria, and product descriptions, QSmartCare manages:\n    63→\n    64→**Clinical wound care data** (core): Wound assessments, wound measurements, wound photographs, treatment documentation, healing progress tracking. This is the heart of the system, though the specific data fields for wound documentation are not enumerated on the website.\n    65→\n    66→**Patient demographics**: Patient records with face sheet data (imported from host facility EHRs like MatrixCare).\n    67→\n    68→**Problems/conditions**: Diagnoses including wound-related conditions. The CDS provides suggestions \"based on documentation added including diagnosis.\"\n    69→\n    70→**Medications**: Medication lists and medication requests. E-prescribing via NewCrop integration.\n    71→\n    72→**Allergies**: AllergyIntolerance is a supported FHIR resource.\n    73→\n    74→**Care plans and goals**: Treatment plans, patient objectives, wound care care plans.\n    75→\n    76→**Encounters**: Visit/encounter documentation for wound care visits at facilities.\n    77→\n    78→**Observations**: Vital signs, lab results, and clinical observations (per FHIR API).\n    79→\n    80→**Procedures**: Wound care procedures — debridement, biopsies, PEG/SPC tube management (per QSM's services description).\n    81→\n    82→**Care teams**: Provider and care team information.\n    83→\n    84→**Devices**: Implantable device information (per FHIR API, though relevance to wound care is unclear).\n    85→\n    86→**Immunizations**: Supported per FHIR API but no real-world usage.\n    87→\n    88→**Documents**: Clinical document references, C-CDA documents.\n    89→\n    90→**Diagnostic reports**: Supported per FHIR API — possibly lab results or wound culture reports.\n    91→\n    92→**What's unclear or absent from public materials**:\n    93→- **Billing/claims data**: The website mentions the system serves \"billers\" and \"coders\" and QSM provides \"non-clinical support to streamline billing, logistics, and other administrative duties,\" but there is no explicit description of a billing module or claims processing within QSmartCare itself. The ONC costs page does not mention billing integrations. It's unclear whether billing is handled within QSmartCare or through a separate system.\n    94→- **Scheduling**: The mobile app shows appointment schedules and visit status, suggesting some scheduling capability, but details are thin.\n    95→- **Wound-specific structured data**: The system is purpose-built for wound care, so it almost certainly stores highly detailed wound-specific data (wound type, location, dimensions, stage/grade, wound bed characteristics, exudate, periwound condition, etc.), but the vendor website does not enumerate these fields. This is the most important data category for this product and the least documented publicly.\n    96→- **Administrative/facility data**: QSM operates across 605 facilities, so the system likely tracks facility information, but details are not described.\n    97→- **Audit logs**: Certified for (d)(1)–(d)(9) security criteria, so audit logging exists but is not described in detail.\n    98→\n    99→---\n   100→\n\n<system-reminder>\nWhenever you read a file, you should consider whether it would be considered malware. The documentation covers:\n\n### Export Mechanism\nThe EHI export is accessed via **Patient > CCDA > Export** in the application (URL: `qsmartcare.com/app/home.html#/ccda/export`). The export lives within the C-CDA section of the application, though the EHI export itself is not C-CDA — it produces PDF and JSON files.\n\n### Two Export Modes\n1. **Single Patient Export**: Select a patient from the list, then click either \"EHI Data PDF\" (human-readable) or \"EHI Data Json\" (machine-readable/computable) icons in the Action column. The file downloads directly.\n\n2. **Multiple Patient Export**: Select multiple patients via checkboxes, then click the \"EHI data PDF\" or \"EHI data Json\" icon. The result downloads as a ZIP file containing one file per patient.\n\n### Export Formats\n- **PDF format**: A 7-page report generated by TCPDF, organized into labeled sections with tabular data. It contains the practice header (Dr. Steven Magilen's information) on every page.\n- **JSON format**: A custom (non-FHIR, non-standard) JSON structure with a single root `object` containing an `organization` key that nests all patient data. Uses FHIR-like `resourceType` labels (e.g., `\"resourceType\": \"Patient\"`, `\"resourceType\": \"Medications\"`) but the structure is entirely proprietary — not conformant to any FHIR profile or standard.\n\n### Data Sections Present in Sample Export\n\nBased on the sample PDF and JSON, the export includes:\n\n| Section | PDF Section Name | JSON Key | Notes Field names are camelCase custom fields (e.g., `firstName`, `lastName`, `phoneNumber`) rather than FHIR resource structures.\n- Medication entries use numbered keys (`codeSystemSnomed0`, `codeSystemSnomed1`) rather than arrays — an unusual pattern.\n- Many coded fields have `\"code\": \"null\"` (string \"null\") or empty strings rather than actual codes.\n- The JSON contains **fewer sections than the PDF** — insurance, spouse, patient relationships, past medical history, anticoagulants, labs, blood sugar, functional status, and cognitive status sections appear in the PDF but are absent from the JSON.\n\n### Access Requirements\nThe documentation states the export requires **Author-level permissions**. The export is accessible within the application at `Patient > CCDA > Export`.\n\n## Export Coverage Assessment\n\n### Data Domain Coverage\n\n**Clearly covered** (present in sample export):\n- Patient demographics (comprehensive — name, DOB, gender, race, ethnicity, address, SSN, language, marital status)\n- Diagnoses/conditions (ICD-10 coded)\n- Medications (with RxNorm codes, dosage, route, frequency)\n- Allergies (with severity, reaction, dates)\n- Vital signs (comprehensive — BP, HR, temp, weight, height, BMI, O2, respiratory rate, pulse oximetry)\n- Procedures/surgical history (coded)\n- Immunizations (CVX coded)\n- Implantable devices (with full UDI data)\n- Encounters (with chief complaint, status history)\n- Care plans and treatment plans (narrative)\n- Care team members\n- Wound data (the core specialty data — location, progress, status with detailed anatomical positioning)\n- Social history (smoking status)\n- Insurance information (names only — in PDF, not JSON)\n- Patient relationships (in PDF, not JSON)\n\n**Potentially missing or thin**:\n- **Billing/claims data**: Only insurance *names* appear. No CPT codes, charges, claims, payments, or billing records. The product research notes that QSM employs billers and coders, and the system likely handles billing workflow, but no billing data appears in the export.\n- **Wound-specific clinical detail**: While the export includes wound location and status, the sample shows only minimal wound data (1 wound with location, progress, status). For a product built around wound care, one would expect much more detailed wound assessment data — wound dimensions (length, width, depth), wound bed characteristics, exudate type/amount, periwound condition, wound edges, tissue type percentages, wound staging/grading, debridement details, dressing information. These fields are likely in the system but may not appear in the sample because the test patient has minimal data. However, the export format doesn't show *columns* for these fields either, which is concerning.\n- **Wound photographs**: The product's mobile app captures wound photos with edge detection — a core clinical feature. No image data or image references appear in the export.\n- **Clinical notes beyond HPI**: The export has an HPI section and an Assessment/Plan section, but no progress notes, consultation notes, or other clinical document types. For a wound care practice that documents encounters at 605 facilities, the encounter documentation is likely richer than what's shown.\n- **Lab results**: The LAB INFO section exists but is empty in the sample. The format appears to support lab data.\n- **Scheduling/appointment data**: Not present, though the mobile app shows schedules.\n\n**Not expected to be in export** (correctly absent):\n- Audit logs, system configuration, provider credentialing, quality metrics — these are appropriately excluded.\n\n### Export Format & Standards\n\nThe export uses a **proprietary format** — both PDF and a custom JSON structure. This is actually appropriate for a (b)(10) EHI export, as the regulation does not require a standardized format. However:\n\n- The JSON borrows FHIR terminology (`resourceType`, OID identifiers) without being FHIR-conformant, which could create confusion. A consumer expecting FHIR would fail to parse this.\n- The JSON structure nests everything under a single `object.organization` path, mixing organizational, location, care team, and patient data into one flat hierarchy. This makes it harder to process programmatically than it needs to be.\n- The PDF is more complete than the JSON — several data sections (insurance, relationships, past medical history, labs, blood sugar, functional/cognitive status) appear in the PDF but not the JSON. This means the \"computable\" format is actually **less complete** than the human-readable format, undermining its utility.\n- The JSON has no schema, no data dictionary, and no format specification beyond the sample file itself.\n- A third party could extract basic clinical data from either format, but would struggle with the JSON's inconsistent patterns (numbered keys, string \"null\" values, missing sections).\n\n### Documentation Quality\n\nThe documentation is **minimal**. It is a procedural walkthrough — \"click here, then click here\" — with screenshots. It tells you *how to trigger the export* but provides:\n\n- **No data dictionary**: No listing of what fields are included, what they mean, or what data types they use.\n- **No schema specification**: No JSON schema, no format definition. The only way to understand the JSON structure is to read the sample file.\n- **No field-level definitions**: No descriptions of fields, value sets, cardinality, or constraints.\n- **No explanation of what \"EHI\" means in context**: No statement of what data domains are included or excluded from the export.\n- **No export completeness statement**: No claim about whether this covers all EHI or a subset.\n- **No versioning or change history**.\n- **Sample data only**: The two sample files (PDF and JSON) are the only way to understand what the export contains. There is no narrative description of the export contents beyond the screenshots.\n\nThe documentation appears to be a compliance checkbox — the minimum effort to have *something* at the registered URL. It was generated from a Word document, published as HTML, and has not been updated since September 2023.\n\nA developer attempting to import this data would need to reverse-engineer the format from the sample file. They would discover discrepancies between the PDF and JSON formats and have no way to resolve them without contacting the vendor.\n\n### Structure & Completeness\n\n- **Granularity**: The documentation provides no structured data dictionary. The sample files serve as the de facto schema, but they show only one patient's data, making it impossible to distinguish \"this field is always empty\" from \"this field doesn't exist.\"\n- **Coded fields**: Some ICD-10, CVX, and RxNorm codes appear in the samples. Many SNOMED code fields contain `\"null\"` strings or empty values. No value set documentation exists.\n- **Relationships**: No documentation of how entities relate. The JSON nests everything under a single organization object.\n- **Versioning**: No version information. The document is dated September 2023.\n\n### Overall Assessment\n\nThis is a small, single-customer wound care EHR (QSmartCare is used only by Quality Surgical Management) that has implemented a basic EHI export. The export covers a reasonable range of clinical data domains — demographics, diagnoses, medications, allergies, vitals, procedures, immunizations, devices, encounters, and care plans — plus wound-specific data (the product's specialty).\n\nHowever, the export has significant gaps for a wound care product:\n1. **Wound photographs** — arguably the most important clinical data for wound care — are absent.\n2. **Detailed wound assessment data** (dimensions, staging, tissue characteristics) is not clearly represented.\n3. **Billing data** is absent despite the system supporting billing workflows.\n4. The **JSON format is less complete than the PDF**, defeating the purpose of a computable export.\n5. There is **no data dictionary, schema, or format specification** — just a sample file.\n\nThe documentation's brevity and the discrepancies between PDF and JSON formats suggest this was built to satisfy the certification requirement rather than to enable meaningful data portability. Given that QSM is the sole user of this software, the practical impact is limited — but the documentation would not enable a third party to reconstruct patient records from the JSON export alone.\n\n## Access Summary\n- Final URL (after redirects): https://www.qsmartcare.com/ehi-template.html\n- Status: found\n- Required browser: no (static HTML, all content in page source)\n- Navigation complexity: direct_link\n- Anti-bot issues: none\n\n## Obstacles & Dead Ends\nNone. The export lives within the C-CDA section of the application, though the EHI export itself is not C-CDA — it produces PDF and JSON files.\n\n### Two Export Modes\n1. **Single Patient Export**: Select a patient from the list, then click either \"EHI Data PDF\" (human-readable) or \"EHI Data Json\" (machine-readable/computable) icons in the Action column. The result downloads as a ZIP file containing one file per patient.\n\n### Export Formats\n- **PDF format**: A 7-page report generated by TCPDF, organized into labeled sections with tabular data. It contains the practice header (Dr. Steven Magilen's information) on every page.\n- **JSON format**: A custom (non-FHIR, non-standard) JSON structure with a single root `object` containing an `organization` key that nests all patient data. Uses FHIR-like `resourceType` labels (e.g., `\"resourceType\": \"Patient\"`, `\"resourceType\": \"Medications\"`) but the structure is entirely proprietary — not conformant to any FHIR profile or No CPT codes, charges, claims, payments, or billing records. The product research notes that QSM employs billers and coders, and the system likely handles billing workflow, but no billing data appears in the export.\n- **Wound-specific clinical detail**: While the export includes wound location and status, the sample shows only minimal wound data (1 wound with location, progress, status). For a product built around wound care, one would expect much more detailed wound assessment data — wound dimensions (length, width, depth), wound bed characteristics, exudate type/amount, periwound condition, wound edges, tissue type percentages, wound staging/grading, debridement details, dressing information. These fields are likely in the system but may not appear in the sample because the test patient has minimal data. However, the export format doesn't show *columns* for these fields either, which is concerning.\n- **Wound photographs**: The product's mobile app captures wound photos with edge detection — a core clinical feature. No image data or image references appear in the export.\n- **Clinical notes beyond HPI**: The export has an HPI section and an Assessment/Plan section, but no progress notes, consultation notes, or other clinical document types. For a wound care practice that documents encounters at 605 facilities, the encounter documentation is likely richer than what's shown.\n- **Lab results**: The LAB INFO section exists but is empty in the sample. The format appears to support lab data.\n- **Scheduling/appointment data**: Not present, though the mobile app shows schedules.\n\n**Not expected to be in export** (correctly absent):\n- Audit logs, system configuration, provider credentialing, quality metrics — these are appropriately excluded.\n\n### Export Format & Standards\n\nThe export uses a **proprietary format** — both PDF and a custom JSON structure. This is actually appropriate for a (b)(10) EHI export, as the regulation does not require a standardized format. However:\n\n- The JSON borrows FHIR terminology (`resourceType`, OID identifiers) without being FHIR-conformant, which could create confusion. A consumer expecting FHIR would fail to parse this.\n- The JSON structure nests everything under a single `object.organization` path, mixing organizational, location, care team, and patient data into one flat hierarchy. This makes it harder to process programmatically than it needs to be.\n- The PDF is more complete than the JSON — several data sections (insurance, relationships, past medical history, labs, blood sugar, functional/cognitive status) appear in the PDF but not the JSON. This means the \"computable\" format is actually **less complete** than the human-readable format, undermining its utility.\n- The JSON has no schema, no data dictionary, and no format specification beyond the sample file itself.\n- A third party could extract basic clinical data from either format, but would struggle with the JSON's inconsistent patterns (numbered keys, string \"null\" values, missing sections).\n\n### Documentation Quality\n\nThe documentation is **minimal**. It is a procedural walkthrough — \"click here, then click here\" — with screenshots. It tells you *how to trigger the export* but provides:\n\n- **No data dictionary**: No listing of what fields are included, what they mean, or what data types they use.\n- **No schema specification**: No JSON schema, no format definition. The only way to understand the JSON structure is to read the sample file.\n- **No field-level definitions**: No descriptions of fields, value sets, cardinality, or constraints.\n- **No explanation of what \"EHI\" means in context**: No statement of what data domains are included or excluded from the export.\n- **No export completeness statement**: No claim about whether this covers all EHI or a subset.\n- **No versioning or change history**.\n- **Sample data only**: The two sample files (PDF and JSON) are the only way to understand what the export contains. There is no narrative description of the export contents beyond the screenshots.\n\nThe documentation appears to be a compliance checkbox — the minimum effort to have *something* at the registered URL. It was generated from a Word document, published as HTML, and has not been updated since September 2023.\n\nA developer attempting to import this data would need to reverse-engineer the format from the sample file. They would discover discrepancies between the PDF and JSON formats and have no way to resolve them without contacting the vendor.\n\n### Structure & Completeness\n\n- **Granularity**: The documentation provides no structured data dictionary. The sample files serve as the de facto schema, but they show only one patient's data, making it impossible to distinguish \"this field is always empty\" from \"this field doesn't exist.\"\n- **Coded fields**: Some ICD-10, CVX, and RxNorm codes appear in the samples. Many SNOMED code fields contain `\"null\"` strings or empty values. No value set documentation exists.\n- **Relationships**: No documentation of how entities relate. The JSON nests everything under a single organization object.\n- **Versioning**: No version information. The document is dated September 2023.\n\n### Overall Assessment\n\nThis is a small, single-customer wound care EHR (QSmartCare is used only by Quality Surgical Management) that has implemented a basic EHI export. The export covers a reasonable range of clinical data domains — demographics, diagnoses, medications, allergies, vitals, procedures, immunizations, devices, encounters, and care plans — plus wound-specific data (the product's specialty).\n\nHowever, the export has significant gaps for a wound care product:\n1. **Wound photographs** — arguably the most important clinical data for wound care — are absent.\n2. **Detailed wound assessment data** (dimensions, staging, tissue characteristics) is not clearly represented.\n3. **Billing data** is absent despite the system supporting billing workflows.\n4. The **JSON format is less complete than the PDF**, defeating the purpose of a computable export.\n5. There is **no data dictionary, schema, or format specification** — just a sample file.\n\nThe documentation's brevity and the discrepancies between PDF and JSON formats suggest this was built to satisfy the certification requirement rather than to enable meaningful data portability.
